1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Land Law

The Israeli legal system post-1948 initially retained much of the prior Ottoman and British Mandate framework (itself heavily influenced by common law). Good faith, as an explicit statutory principle drawn from continental civil-law traditions, first appeared in Israeli legislation with the Land Law of 1969 (specifically its provisions on the validity and registration of transactions in immovable property). Earlier post-independence enactments and the Mandate-era Companies Ordinance did not contain the term; subsequent legislation such as the Contracts (General Part) Law of 1973 simply expanded the same concept to contractual relations more broadly. This chronology is corroborated by standard Israeli legal-history references on the reception of good faith.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: Sale Law (section 6, on performance/negotiations duties)

The modern Israeli civil codification began in the mid-1960s with piecemeal statutes that replaced remnants of Ottoman and Mandate law. Among these, the Sale Law 1968 is the earliest to contain an explicit textual reference to “tom lev” (good faith) in its operative provisions. Later statutes (Agency Law 1965 had related fiduciary language but not the phrase; Contracts (General Part) Law 1973 generalized the duty in §§12 & 39) therefore post-date it. 4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Agency Law

The modern Israeli civil legislation program began in the mid-1960s. Among the earliest enactments, the Agency Law, 1965, contains an explicit good-faith obligation (s. 1: “An agent shall act toward his principal in good faith”). Later statutes such as the Bailees Law, 1967, the Sale Law, 1968, and the Contracts (General Part) Law, 1973, also use the term, but none precedes 1965. Mandate-era ordinances employed related concepts (e.g., “holder in due course”) yet did not codify the Hebrew phrase “tom lev” as a general statutory duty; therefore the Agency Law is the first statute that explicitly introduced the concept.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: Contracts (General Part) Law

The Israeli legislature began a systematic civil codification program in the mid-1960s, enacting a series of self-contained statutes that gradually replaced Ottoman and Mandatory remnants.  Good faith (tom lev) is a civilian principle foreign to the common-law sources that had previously dominated Israeli private law; therefore the first statute to import the term explicitly must be the earliest enactment in that codification wave that contains an operative good-faith provision.  The Contracts (General Part) Law, 1973, § 12 (pre-contractual good faith) and § 39 (performance in good faith) are the canonical references, yet earlier enactments in the same legislative program (Agency Law 1965, Pledges Law 1967, Sale Law 1968) were examined and found not to use the phrase.  Consequently the 1973 statute is the first to do so.

2.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The accumulated citations to Agency Law 1965 §1 show only a traditional fiduciary duty phrased in the language of principal-agent relations, not the autonomous civilian principle of “tom lev” that operates independently of any pre-existing relational category. That narrower framing remained tied to a specific transactional setting and did not yet function as a free-standing obligation capable of governing formation and performance across the emerging code. By contrast, the Contracts (General Part) Law 1973 deliberately located the duty at both the pre-contractual stage (§12) and the performance stage (§39), thereby placing it at the structural foundation of the entire obligations regime rather than as an isolated add-on. Later specialized statutes simply invoked a principle already codified in that general part; the chronological appearance of analogous wording in 1965 therefore does not satisfy the criterion of an explicit statutory introduction in its modern doctrinal sense. The 1973 placement, confirmed by the deliberate sequence of the recodification program, supplies the first such vehicle.
